questions.q: State the three postulates of cell theory as proposed by Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow.
questions.a: The three postulates are: (1) All living organisms are composed of one or more cells. (2) The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in living organisms. (3) All cells arise from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula e cellula). A wrong answer that omits Virchow's postulate or confuses 'structure' with 'function' reveals the student memorized a list without understanding that the third postulate was a later, critical addition that refuted spontaneous generation.

questions.q: Why was Schleiden's conclusion that 'all plants are made of cells' (1838) and Schwann's extension to animals (1839) considered a unification of biology? Explain using the concept of 'levels of organisation'.
questions.a: Before cell theory, plants and animals were studied as separate kingdoms with no structural commonality. Schleiden and Schwann showed that despite vast differences in form (e.g., a mango tree vs. a goat), both are built from the same fundamental unit — the cell. This placed the 'cell' as the common base level in the hierarchy: cell → tissue → organ → organism, unifying botany and zoology. A wrong answer that only says 'they both studied cells' misses the conceptual leap: the cell became the *reference point* for comparing life processes across kingdoms.

questions.q: A student argues: "Viruses have genetic material and evolve, so they should be considered living cells according to cell theory." Use the postulates of cell theory to evaluate this claim.
questions.a: Step 1: Recall postulate 1 — all living organisms are composed of cells. Step 2: Observe that a virus particle (virion) is acellular — it lacks cytoplasm, organelles, and a cell membrane. Step 3: Recall postulate 2 — the cell is the basic unit of function. Viruses cannot metabolize or reproduce independently; they hijack host cells. Step 4: Recall postulate 3 — cells arise from pre-existing cells. Viruses are assembled from synthesized components inside a host, not by division of a parent virus. Conclusion: Viruses violate all three postulates; they are non-living infectious particles. A wrong answer that focuses only on 'genetic material' ignores that cell theory defines life by *cellular organization*, not just heredity.

questions.q: Compare the evidence available to Schleiden (plant cells) and Schwann (animal cells) in the 1830s. Why was it harder for Schwann to convince zoologists than for Schleiden to convince botanists?
questions.a: Schleiden studied plant tissues (e.g., onion epidermis, cork) which have rigid cell walls, making cells easily visible and clearly demarcated even with simple microscopes. Animal cells lack cell walls; they are smaller, fragile, and often embedded in extracellular matrix, making boundaries blurry. Schwann had to rely on cartilage cells (chondrocytes) in lacunae — the only animal cells with clear borders. Zoologists argued animal 'cells' were just nuclei in a common blastema. A wrong answer that says 'plants are simpler' misses the technical point: cell walls provided *visible evidence* of cellular individuality that animal cells lacked.

questions.q: In 1855, Virchow added the third postulate: 'Omnis cellula e cellula'. Evaluate how this single statement transformed cell theory from a *structural description* into a *dynamic principle* of biology.
questions.a: The first two postulates described *what* living things are made of (static structure). Virchow's postulate described *how* life continues (dynamic process). It linked cell theory to reproduction, growth, repair, and heredity — all explained by cell division. It also refuted spontaneous generation (life from non-life) by asserting continuity of cellular lineage. A wrong answer that treats it as just 'another fact about cells' fails to see that it made cell theory *explanatory* for life cycles, development, and disease (e.g., cancer as uncontrolled cell division).

questions.q: Design a simple investigation using materials from a typical Indian kitchen/garden to demonstrate *one* postulate of cell theory to a Class 6 student. Specify the material, method, observation, and which postulate it supports.
questions.a: Material: Onion peel (epidermis) and a drop of curd (dahi). Method: Mount onion peel in water on a slide; observe under microscope. Then mount a drop of diluted curd; observe. Observation: Onion peel shows rectangular plant cells with clear walls and nuclei. Curd shows numerous tiny rod-shaped bacteria (Lactobacillus) moving actively. Postulate supported: Postulate 1 — 'All living organisms are composed of cells.' The onion (plant) and bacteria (microorganism) are both made of cells, visible to the student. A poor answer uses only one specimen (e.g., only onion) and cannot show the *universality* of the postulate across kingdoms.
